Converting an SS3 model to opal

A step-by-step guide, worked through with the IO yellowfin SS3 model

Author

Nicholas Ducharme-Barth

Published

October 15, 2026

1 Purpose

This guide shows how a Stock Synthesis 3 (SS3) assessment is converted into an opal model, how to test that the conversion is right, and how to set up and fit the opal model. It works through one example from start to finish: the IATTC team’s SS3 model of the Indian Ocean yellowfin (IO YFT) simulated data, which became opal fit C2. It is written for analysts converting their own SS3 model, and section 9 lists what to compare between your model and this one.

All the code is in one companion script, code/rtmb/scripts/05-io-yft-ss3-to-opal-workflow.r. The code shown below is taken from that script, not retyped. Copy the script and edit it for your model. The results here are from the script’s own run, read from the cache it writes.

This guide covers the workflow only. For how the opal fits compare with SS3 and with the simulated truth, and why they differ, see:

  • ss3-to-opal-io-yft.qmd: the first conversion, with both biology routes, diagnostic fits and the comparison with the operating model.
  • ss3-to-opal-io-yft-age-k.qmd: SS3’s age-specific K growth in opal, and the selectivity fits C and C2.
  • code/rtmb/sims/sims-synthesis.qmd: simulations of the catch-timing and selectivity differences between the two platforms.

1.1 How the converter works

The converter is a set of R functions in code/rtmb/helper-fns/:

File What it does
ss3-read.R Reads the SS3 files with r4ss and records their checksums
ss3-convert.R Converts dimensions, fleets, catch, indices, length compositions, selectivity and parameters (ss3_to_opal())
ss3-biology.R Converts biology and growth: M, weight, maturity, spawning potential, length-at-age
ss3-validate.R Tests: structural checks, reconciliation with SS3, the bridging replay
ss3-opal-obj.R Builds the opal object and switches selectivity between SS3’s and opal’s
ss3-fit-tools.R Newton polishing after nlminb, and extraction helpers

The converter follows three rules:

  1. Derived quantities come from Report.sso wherever SS3 reports them: M, weight, maturity and spawning potential at age, selectivity at age, unfished spawning biomass and the recruitment bias ramp. These quantities already include every transformation SS3 applied internally, so nothing has to be re-derived from the control file.
  2. Every decision that cannot be read from the SS3 files is in one settings list. That includes how to split an index, which fleets’ compositions to use and which opal curve to use for each fleet. The functions hard-code nothing about the model.
  3. Where opal cannot represent SS3 exactly, the converter reports how close it gets rather than hiding the approximation.

The workflow has eight steps:

Step Section Main functions Output
1. Settings 3 an R list cfg
2. Read SS3 4 ss3_read_model() ss3
3. Convert 5 ss3_to_opal(), prep_lf_data() converted
4. Test inputs 6.1–6.2 validate_opal_inputs(), ss3_reconcile() check tables
5. Build 6.3 ss3_opal_obj() assessment
6. Test dynamics 6.4–6.5 ss3_use_external_selectivity(), ss3_bridge_table() bridging table
7. Set up and fit 7 ss3_seed_par_sel(), ss3_use_estimated_selectivity(), opal_fit() fit
8. Inspect and save 7–8 opal_report(), opal_save() results, saved fit

2 What you need

  • R with opal ≥ 0.1.1 (dev branch; 0.1.1 adds SS3’s age-specific K growth), r4ss, data.table, magrittr and this.path.
  • The SS3 model folder, with these files from a converged run:
    • data.ss_new (data);
    • control.ss_new (control);
    • ss3.par (parameter estimates; called ss.par in some versions);
    • Report.sso, which the converter needs for biology, selectivity and B0.
  • The converter functions (code/rtmb/helper-fns/).
library(data.table)
library(magrittr)
library(opal)
library(r4ss)

stopifnot("opal >= 0.1.1 is required for SS3 age-specific K growth" =
              utils::packageVersion("opal") >= "0.1.1")
proj_dir = this.path::this.proj()
dir_fns  = file.path(proj_dir, "code", "rtmb", "helper-fns")
dir_out  = file.path(proj_dir, "code", "rtmb", "vignettes", "data")
dir.create(dir_out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# The converter: ss3-read.R, ss3-convert.R, ss3-biology.R, ss3-validate.R,
# ss3-opal-obj.R and ss3-fit-tools.R.
for (f in list.files(dir_fns, pattern = "\\.[Rr]$", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)

3 The conversion settings

Everything the converter needs to know beyond the SS3 files is in cfg, a plain R list. The table below lists each block. The values below are for IO YFT, and each needs to be checked again for another model.

Block Decision IO YFT choice
time Which SS3 time steps become opal time steps All 256; each SS3 “year” is a quarter, so opal has n_year = 256, n_season = 1
age Which SS3 ages to keep 1–28, so the opal age equals the SS3 age (age 0 dropped)
growth How opal computes length-at-age ss3_age_k: SS3’s GrowthModel 3 reproduced exactly
bio Where M, weight, maturity and spawning potential come from endgrowth: Report.sso’s age table, used directly
index How SS3’s index fleets map to opal index series Fleet 17 split into four quarterly series (opal 17–20)
lf Which fleets’ length compositions to use, and the bin grid Fleets 1–14 and 16; last bin regularised to 195–200 cm
selectivity opal curve per fishery, and which parameters to estimate Double-normal for fisheries, logistic for the index; estimate what SS3 estimated 
# Every choice that cannot be read from the SS3 files. The converter reads
# nothing else, so this list is the full record of the conversion decisions.
cfg = list(
    model       = "io-yft-sim-iattc-sample-tree-4",
    # SS3 model folder, relative to dir_root in ss3_to_opal() (or set
    # absolute_paths = TRUE and give a full path).
    ss3_dir     = "model-files/ss3/xx-io-yft-sim-iattc-sample-tree-4",
    ss3_version = "3.24",
    files = list(
        dat         = "data.ss_new",
        ctl         = "control.ss_new",
        par         = "ss3.par",
        read_report = TRUE        # Report.sso: endgrowth, ageselex, SSB0, bias ramp
    ),

    # Time: 256 SS3 "years" that are quarters (nseas = 1, months_per_seas = 3).
    # opal runs the same 256 steps with n_season = 1.
    time = list(first_ts = 1, last_ts = 256),

    # Ages: drop SS3 age 0 so that the opal age index equals the SS3 age.
    age = list(keep_ss3_ages = c(1, 28), min_age = 1),

    # Growth: SS3 GrowthModel 3 (age-specific K) reproduced exactly in opal.
    # "schnute" would instead fit opal's single-k curve to SS3's length-at-age.
    growth = list(
        model             = "ss3_age_k",
        plus_group_adjust = TRUE,   # SS3's plus-group mean length
        A1 = 1, A2 = 28, fit_cv = TRUE   # used only by model = "schnute"
    ),

    # Biology: M, weight, maturity and Mat*Fecund at age straight from SS3's
    # endgrowth table ("control" would rebuild them from the control file).
    bio = list(
        source = "endgrowth",
        endgrowth = list(
            length_basis       = "Beg",
            weight             = TRUE,
            maturity           = TRUE,
            spawning_potential = TRUE,
            apply_frac_female  = FALSE,   # single-sex model: SSB has no female fraction
            m                  = TRUE
        ),
        m_rate_divisor = NULL   # NULL: 12 / (nseas * months_per_seas) = 4 here
    ),

    # Index: SS3 fleet 17 (longline CPUE) split into four quarterly series,
    # opal fisheries 17-20, each with its own catchability.
    index = list(
        keep_ss3_fleets = 17,
        split = list(list(fleet = 17, into = 17:20, by = "ts_modulo",
                          modulo = 4, offset = 81)),
        normalise            = "mean1",
        month_labels         = c(2, 5, 8, 11),
        keep_negative_fleets = FALSE
    ),

    # Length compositions: fleets with length data in SS3; the last SS3 bin
    # (195-198 cm) is regularised onto the 5 cm grid.
    lf = list(
        keep_negative_fleets = FALSE,
        regularise_last_bin  = TRUE,
        keep_fisheries       = c(1:14, 16),
        cap                  = NULL,
        addtocomp            = 1e-10
    ),

    # Selectivity. opal codes (not SS3 patterns): 1 logistic, 2 double-normal,
    # 3 double Richards. Fisheries 1-16 double-normal, index 17-20 logistic.
    selectivity = list(
        report_factor  = "Asel2",   # Report.sso ageselex rows to read
        reference_year = NULL,      # NULL: terminal year
        n_par          = 6,
        opal_type_f    = c(rep(2, 16), rep(1, 4)),
        # Estimate the opal equivalents of the parameters SS3 estimated.
        estimate = c(1:14, 17),
        mirror   = list(`15` = 14, `16` = 14, `18` = 17, `19` = 17, `20` = 17),
        free_par = list(`1` = 1:2, `2` = 1:4),
        # Parameters the length data do not inform (they settled on the prior
        # mean when estimated), held at their seeded values instead.
        fix_prior_dominated = list(`4` = c(2, 4), `5` = c(2, 4), `7` = c(2, 4),
                                   `9` = 4, `13` = c(2, 4))
    ),

    # SS3's generalised size compositions are not converted.
    sizefreq = list(include = FALSE),

    metadata = list(species = "Yellowfin tuna", region = "Indian Ocean",
                    data_type = "simulated")
)
# Provenance stored on the opal object.
cfg$config_path = "code/rtmb/scripts/05-io-yft-ss3-to-opal-workflow.r"
cfg$config_md5  = unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(proj_dir, cfg$config_path)))

Points that are easy to get wrong:

  • Time units. opal’s time step is the model step. When the SS3 year is a quarter, SS3 still reads M and the von Bertalanffy K as annual rates and applies them over the season. The converter divides both by 12 / (nseas × months_per_seas), which is 4 here (bio$m_rate_divisor).
  • Biology route. endgrowth takes biology at age from SS3 exactly. Use control only if growth is to be estimated in opal: it rebuilds weight and maturity on a length basis and converts them through opal’s length-at-age, so any difference in growth then reaches spawning biomass.
  • Selectivity codes. opal_type_f uses opal’s codes (1 logistic, 2 double-normal, 3 double Richards), not SS3 pattern numbers. validate_opal_inputs() checks this.
  • Index splitting is a modelling choice: one SS3 index with one catchability, against four opal series with four. Leave split empty to keep SS3’s index as one series.
  • estimate, mirror, free_par and fix_prior_dominated are used only when the final model is set up (section 7), not during conversion.

4 Read the SS3 model

ss3_to_opal() reads the files itself. Reading them separately first lets you look at the model and record the features that decide how it converts.

# ss3_to_opal() reads the files itself; reading them here as well is for
# looking at the model before converting it.
ss3 = ss3_read_model(dir_ss3     = file.path(proj_dir, cfg$ss3_dir),
                     dat_file    = cfg$files$dat,
                     ctl_file    = cfg$files$ctl,
                     par_file    = cfg$files$par,
                     version     = cfg$ss3_version,
                     read_report = TRUE)
names(ss3)   # dat, ctl, par, rep (r4ss::SS_output) and provenance
# The SS3 features the converter depends on. Run this on your own model and
# compare it with the yellowfin column in the guide.
ss3_model_features = function(ss3) {
    dat = ss3$dat; ctl = ss3$ctl; rep = ss3$rep
    get = function(x, nm, default = NA) {
        hit = intersect(nm, names(x))
        if (length(hit)) x[[hit[1]]] else default
    }
    n_rows = function(x) if (is.null(x) || !length(x)) 0L else NROW(x)
    patterns = function(x) {
        if (is.null(x) || !NROW(x)) return("none")
        p = as.data.frame(x)[[1]]
        paste(sort(unique(p)), collapse = ", ")
    }
    yn = function(x) if (isTRUE(x)) "yes" else "no"
    data.table::data.table(
        feature = c("SS3 version", "Model period (SS3 years)", "Seasons per year",
                    "Months per season", "Sexes", "Areas", "Ages (max)",
                    "Fishing fleets", "Survey / index fleets",
                    "Catch units (1 biomass, 2 numbers)",
                    "Index observations", "Length composition rows",
                    "Age composition rows", "Generalised size comp methods",
                    "Tag release groups", "Growth model (1 vB, 2 Richards, 3 age-K)",
                    "Growth patterns", "Platoons per growth pattern",
                    "Length selectivity patterns", "Age selectivity patterns",
                    "Time-block designs", "F method", "Stock-recruit function",
                    "Report.sso available"),
        value = c(
            as.character(get(rep, "SS_version", get(dat, "ReadVersion", NA))),
            paste(get(dat, "styr"), get(dat, "endyr"), sep = "-"),
            get(dat, "nseas"),
            paste(unique(get(dat, c("months_per_seas", "month_per_seas"))), collapse = ", "),
            get(dat, "Nsexes"),
            get(dat, "N_areas"),
            get(dat, "Nages"),
            get(dat, c("Nfleet", "Nfleets")),
            get(dat, "Nsurveys", 0),
            paste(unique(get(dat, "units_of_catch", NA)), collapse = ", "),
            n_rows(get(dat, "CPUE", NULL)),
            n_rows(get(dat, "lencomp", NULL)),
            n_rows(get(dat, "agecomp", NULL)),
            get(dat, "N_sizefreq_methods", 0),
            get(dat, "N_tag_groups", 0),
            get(ctl, "GrowthModel"),
            get(ctl, "N_GP"),
            get(ctl, "N_platoon", 1),
            patterns(get(ctl, "size_selex_types", NULL)),
            patterns(get(ctl, "age_selex_types", NULL)),
            get(ctl, "N_Block_Designs", 0),
            get(ctl, "F_Method"),
            get(ctl, "SR_function"),
            yn(!is.null(rep))
        )
    )
}
features = ss3_model_features(ss3)
features

ss3_model_features() is defined in the script. Its output for IO YFT is in section 9, next to a blank column for your own model.

5 Convert

converted = ss3_to_opal(cfg, dir_root = proj_dir)
names(converted)   # data, parameters, lf, selectivity, meta, ss3

# Length compositions go into the data list through opal's prep_lf_data().
# SS3's mult_by_lencomp_N becomes opal's lf_var_adjust (its reciprocal).
lf_wide = dcast(converted$lf, fishery + year + month + ts ~ bin,
                value.var = "value", fill = 0) %>%
          setorder(fishery, ts) %>%
          as.data.frame()                 # opal objects cannot hold data.tables
converted$data = prep_lf_data(
    converted$data, lf_wide,
    lf_switch         = 1L,
    lf_keep_fisheries = as.integer(cfg$lf$keep_fisheries),
    lf_var_adjust     = converted$meta$lf_var_adjust,
    lf_cap            = cfg$lf$cap,
    lf_addtocomp      = cfg$lf$addtocomp
) %>% ss3_make_portable()

ss3_to_opal() returns:

  • data: the opal data list;
  • parameters: starting values at SS3’s estimates;
  • lf: length compositions in long format;
  • selectivity: SS3’s selectivity-at-age, and the same projected onto length bins;
  • meta: diagnostics and provenance;
  • ss3: the r4ss objects it read.

The starting values are SS3’s own estimates:

  • log_B0 is SS3’s unfished spawning biomass (opal estimates B0, not R0).
  • rdev_y holds SS3’s recruitment deviations.
  • Steepness and σR come from the par file.
  • Growth comes from the SS3 files.
  • Each fishery’s initial F is set to effectively zero (log_init_F_f), so the model starts unfished.
  • Catchabilities start at 1.

Then prep_lf_data() (an opal function) adds the length compositions to the data list. SS3’s mult_by_lencomp_N becomes opal’s lf_var_adjust; opal divides the sample size by it, so the converter passes the reciprocal.

Two opal rules affect anything you add to the data list:

  • Only plain R objects. opal_obj() rejects data elements that hold an external pointer, and every data.table has one. Convert to data.frame (as above) or run ss3_make_portable() on the list.
  • Change an opal object only through opal_update(). The object stores a hash of its contents. Assigning directly (x$data$foo <- ...) makes the next validation fail with “Model state was modified directly”. The ss3_use_*() helpers all go through opal_update().

6 Test the conversion

The tests run in order, from the cheapest and most specific to the most general. A failure at one level should be fixed before moving on, because the later tests cannot separate a conversion error from a real difference between the two models.

Test Asks Fails when
1. Structure Is the opal input internally consistent? dimension mismatches, wrong codes, non-portable objects
2. Reconciliation Did the data and biology survive the conversion? lost or duplicated observations, wrong units, wrong female fraction
3. Build Can opal evaluate the model at the starting values? non-finite objective or gradient
4. Bridging At SS3’s parameters, does opal reproduce SS3’s dynamics? any remaining conversion error that affects the population

6.1 Test 1: structure

# Test 1: is the opal input internally consistent?
checks = validate_opal_inputs(converted, strict = FALSE)
checks[, .(n_checks = .N, passed = sum(pass))]
checks[pass == FALSE]

validate_opal_inputs() checks the following:

  • dimensions (ages, years, fisheries, length bins);
  • that M, weight, maturity and spawning potential have a valid length and range;
  • catch array shape and units codes;
  • index columns, index numbering and time window;
  • length composition bins and fisheries;
  • parameter vector lengths;
  • selectivity codes;
  • that nothing non-portable is in the data list.

For IO YFT, 38 of 38 checks pass.

Check Pass

endgrowth route supplies maturity on an age basis yes

6.2 Test 2: reconciliation with SS3

# Test 2: did the data and biology survive the conversion?
recon = ss3_reconcile(converted, tol = 1e-6)
recon[, .(quantity, ss3, opal, rel_diff, pass)]

ss3_reconcile() compares quantities that should match SS3 exactly. Each has a relative tolerance of 10-6, except spawning potential per recruit, which has 10-4. The most informative row is unfished spawning potential per recruit: one number that would show M in the wrong time units (a factor of about 4 here), a misplaced female fraction (a factor of 2) or a wrong plus-group treatment. Its small residual comes from two places: Report.sso prints six significant figures, and SS3 3.24 closes the plus group differently from opal.

The length-at-age row compares opal’s growth (get_growth() with SS3’s parameters and K multipliers) with SS3’s Len_Beg. Its error is at the level of Report.sso’s print precision, so the growth conversion is exact. With growth$model = "schnute" this row would report how well a single-k curve approximates SS3’s growth.

6.3 Test 3: build the opal object

# The opal assessment object. ss3_opal_obj() adds opal's default priors and
# the SS3 provenance, and opal_build() checks that the objective and gradient
# are finite at the starting values (the converted SS3 optimum).
assessment = ss3_opal_obj(converted, cfg,
                          control = list(eval.max = 10000, iter.max = 10000),
                          build   = TRUE)
summary(assessment)

ss3_opal_obj() does three things:

  • attaches opal’s default priors (get_priors());
  • records the SS3 file checksums, r4ss version and settings in $provenance$metadata;
  • runs opal_build(), which builds the RTMB tape and checks that the objective and gradient are finite at the starting values.

The default map (get_map()) estimates log_B0, the recruitment deviations and the catchabilities, and fixes growth and selectivity.

6.4 Test 4: bridging at SS3’s parameters

This is the main test of the conversion. SS3’s selectivity-at-age is put into opal directly (sel_fa_external), every parameter is left at SS3’s value, and nothing is estimated. opal’s spawning biomass is then compared with SS3’s.

# Test 3: with SS3's own selectivity-at-age and parameters, does opal
# reproduce SS3's spawning biomass? Nothing is estimated here.
bridge_obj = ss3_use_external_selectivity(
    assessment, converted$selectivity$sel_fa_external) %>%
    opal_build()
bridge = ss3_bridge_table(converted, opal_report(bridge_obj))
# ss3: SS3 SSB. opal: opal at SS3's values. replica_ss3: the same converted
# inputs replayed with SS3's catch and recruitment timing.
bridge[, .(series   = c("opal", "replay with SS3 timing"),
           max_abs  = c(max(abs(rel_opal)), max(abs(rel_replica_ss3))),
           mean_abs = c(mean(abs(rel_opal)), mean(abs(rel_replica_ss3))))]

Even with every input converted exactly, the two models differ in two places:

  • Catch timing. opal removes each step’s catch at the start of the step, before natural mortality. SS3 applies fishing and natural mortality together through the Baranov equation.
  • Recruitment timing. opal recruits the first age class at t + 1 from spawning biomass at t + 1. With SS3 age 0 dropped, SS3’s matching fish were recruited from spawning biomass at t.

ss3_bridge_replica() replays the population on the converted inputs, either with opal’s timing or with SS3’s:

  • With opal’s timing it reproduces opal_report().
  • With SS3’s timing it should reproduce SS3’s spawning biomass.

A small residual under SS3’s timing shows that the conversion is correct. Any gap left between opal and SS3 is then a real difference between the platforms, not a conversion error.

Series Mean |difference| from SS3 Max |difference| from SS3
opal at SS3 values 2.54% 10.28%
converted inputs, replayed with SS3 timing 0.09% 0.44%

For IO YFT, opal at SS3’s values differs from SS3 by up to 10.3%. The replay with SS3’s timing differs by at most 0.44%. The conversion is therefore correct, and the opal–SS3 gap at fixed parameters comes from catch timing. The simulations in code/rtmb/sims/ measure how much that timing difference matters in estimation.

If the replay with SS3’s timing does not match SS3, look for a conversion error. Common causes:

  • catch units (biomass vs numbers) or a fleet out of order;
  • M or K not rescaled to the time step;
  • a female fraction applied twice or not at all;
  • selectivity read for the wrong fleet, year or Factor (Asel vs Asel2);
  • recruitment deviations misaligned by a step.

The replay needs biology at age and SS3’s selectivity, so it works only with the endgrowth route.

6.5 Starting objective and gradient

# Test 4: the starting objective and gradient. A non-finite value or a very
# large gradient points at a parameter or data element on the wrong scale.
start_check = function(x) {
    obj = opal_rtmb(x, fresh = TRUE)
    data.table(n_par = length(obj$par), objective = obj$fn(obj$par),
               max_abs_gradient = max(abs(obj$gr(obj$par))))
}
start_check(bridge_obj)
Configuration Estimated parameters Objective Max |gradient|
bridge (SS3 selectivity) 261 14,242.066 2.72e+02
final (C2) 310 14,920.569 1.43e+03

The objective must be finite. At the converted SS3 optimum, the gradient is not zero, because the two models’ likelihoods differ, but it should not be huge. A very large gradient on one parameter usually means a scale error in that parameter or in the data it fits.

7 Set up and fit the final model

The bridging configuration used SS3’s selectivity as fixed data. The final model, C2, uses opal’s own length-based selectivity curves instead, with the opal equivalent of each parameter SS3 estimated being estimated here too.

7.1 Seed opal’s selectivity from SS3’s

SS3’s selectivity here is on age, while opal’s is on length, and there is no algebraic conversion between the two. ss3_seed_par_sel() projects SS3’s selectivity-at-age onto the length bins using SS3’s age–length key. It then fits each opal curve to that projection by least squares, using opal’s own selectivity functions so that the seeded values are on opal’s scale.

# SS3's selectivity is on age, opal's on length. Starting values come from
# fitting each opal curve to SS3's selectivity projected onto length bins.
seed = ss3_seed_par_sel(
    sel_target_fl = converted$selectivity$sel_target_fl,
    len_mid       = converted$data$len_mid,
    sel_type_f    = converted$data$sel_type_f,
    n_par         = cfg$selectivity$n_par)
data.table(fishery = seq_along(seed$rmse), rmse = round(seed$rmse, 4))
Fishery opal curve RMSE against SS3
1: fishing_gi_1 double-normal 0.026
2: fishing_gi_4 double-normal 0.021
3: fishing_hd_1 double-normal 0.020
4: fishing_ll_1 double-normal 0.014
5: fishing_ll_2 double-normal 0.008
6: fishing_ll_3 double-normal 0.012
7: fishing_ll_4 double-normal 0.015
8: fishing_other_1 double-normal 0.012
9: fishing_other_4 double-normal 0.011
10: fishing_bb_1 double-normal 0.050
11: fishing_ps_1 double-normal 0.007
12: fishing_ps_2 double-normal 0.014
13: fishing_ps_4 double-normal 0.007
14: fishing_trol_1 double-normal 0.015
15: fishing_trol_2 double-normal 0.015
16: fishing_trol_4 double-normal 0.015

18: llcpue_q2 logistic 0.014
19: llcpue_q3 logistic 0.014
20: llcpue_q4 logistic 0.014

The RMSE is on the selectivity scale (0–1) and shows how well the chosen opal curve can follow SS3’s shape. A large value for a fishery means that curve family does not fit SS3’s shape, so change opal_type_f for that fishery before fitting.

7.2 Choose what to estimate

ss3_use_estimated_selectivity() removes SS3’s selectivity from the model, puts in the seeded curves and writes the selectivity part of the map from cfg$selectivity:

  • estimate: fisheries whose curves are estimated. IO YFT: the 14 fishing fleets with their own selectivity in SS3, and the index.
  • free_par: which curve parameters are estimated, by opal curve family. For the double-normal, columns 1–4 (peak, top width, ascending and descending widths) are estimated, as SS3 estimated P1–P4 of its pattern
    1. For the logistic, both parameters are estimated.
  • mirror: fisheries sharing another fishery’s parameters (SS3 pattern 15). Fisheries 15 and 16 mirror 14; the four quarterly index series share one curve.
  • fix: parameters held at their seeded values. In an earlier fit (C), these nine went to the mean of opal’s selectivity prior, which meant the length data did not inform them, so C2 fixes them.
# Fit C2: opal's own length-based selectivity, estimated where SS3 estimated
# it, mirrored where SS3 mirrored it, with the prior-dominated parameters
# fixed. log_B0, the recruitment deviations and the four catchabilities are
# estimated as in opal's default map; growth stays at SS3's values.
final = assessment %>%
    ss3_use_estimated_selectivity(seed$par_sel, cfg,
                                  fix = cfg$selectivity$fix_prior_dominated) %>%
    opal_build()
start_check(final)

# What is estimated: map entries that are not NA.
estimated = rbindlist(lapply(names(final$parameters), function(p) {
    m = final$map[[p]]
    n = if (is.null(m)) length(final$parameters[[p]]) else length(unique(na.omit(m)))
    data.table(parameter = p, n_estimated = n)
}))[n_estimated > 0]
estimated
Parameter Estimated
log_B0 1
log_cpue_q 4
rdev_y 256
par_sel 49

The 310 estimated parameters are log_B0, the 256 recruitment deviations, the four catchabilities and 49 selectivity parameters. Growth, steepness, σR and the observation variances stay at their SS3 or default values (opal’s default map).

7.3 Fit

# Two nlminb passes, then Newton steps to bring the gradient down, then
# opal_check() on the polished optimum.
t0  = proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit = opal_fit(final, n_passes = 2L, check = FALSE)
obj = opal_rtmb(fit, fresh = TRUE)
pol = ss3_newton_polish(obj, fit$fit$opt$par)
opt = fit$fit$opt
opt$par       = setNames(pol$par, names(opt$par))
opt$objective = pol$objective
fit = opal_attach_fit(fit, opt, check = TRUE,
                      check_args = list(gradient_tolerance = 1e-4))
fit_seconds = proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0

convergence = data.table(
    objective_start = start_check(final)$objective,
    objective_fit   = opt$objective,
    max_gradient    = pol$max_gradient,
    newton_steps    = pol$steps,
    check_passes    = isTRUE(fit$validation$fit$passes),
    positive_hessian = isTRUE(fit$validation$fit$metrics$positive_hessian),
    seconds         = fit_seconds)
convergence

opal_fit() runs nlminb (here two passes). nlminb stops on relative change in the objective, which for an objective of this size can leave gradients near 10-3. ss3_newton_polish() then takes a few Newton steps with the exact RTMB Hessian. opal_attach_fit() puts the polished optimum back on the object and runs opal_check(), which checks the gradient (here to 10-4), that the Hessian is positive definite and that the parameters are estimable.

Objective at start Objective at fit Max |gradient| Newton steps Positive definite Hessian opal_check() Seconds
14,920.57 14,406.585 8.0e-12 2 yes passed 103

7.4 Save

fit_path = file.path(dir_out, "io-yft-workflow-fit.rds")
opal_save(fit, fit_path, compress = "xz", overwrite = TRUE)
# Later: fit = opal_read(fit_path, rebuild = TRUE)

opal_save() stores the whole object: data, parameters, map, fit and provenance. opal_read(path, rebuild = TRUE) loads it again and rebuilds the RTMB tape, ready for opal_report().

8 A first look at the fit

These figures only check that the fitted model is sensible and close to SS3. The two vignettes listed in section 1 have the full comparison, including against the simulated truth. The companion script’s results chunk builds these tables from opal_report(fit) and SS3’s Report.sso, and can be reused as it is.

Quantity SS3 opal opal / SS3
B0 (unfished SSB) 4,659,770 4,095,647 0.88
Terminal SSB 1,858,230 1,258,097 0.68
Terminal SSB / B0 0.399 0.307 0.77

For IO YFT, opal’s B0 is 0.88 × SS3’s, and its terminal SSB/B0 is 0.31 against SS3’s 0.40. Most of that gap comes from selectivity. When the same opal model is fitted with SS3’s selectivity-at-age held fixed (fit A1 in ss3-to-opal-io-yft-age-k.qmd), its terminal SSB/B0 is within 0.01 of SS3’s. The remaining sources of difference are:

  • catch timing;
  • opal’s length-based selectivity curves, which cannot match every SS3 age-based shape;
  • the index split into four series with separate catchabilities;
  • SS3 data that opal does not use (here, the survey’s generalised size compositions).

What matters is that the gap can be explained. The two vignettes explain the IO YFT gap one cause at a time.

9 From yellowfin to your model

The converter was written for, and tested on, this one SS3 model. It reads the general SS3 file layout through r4ss, but wherever IO YFT did not need a feature, the code does not handle it. Before converting another model, list its features with ss3_model_features() and compare them with IO YFT’s. Each difference tells you which function to check or extend. The last column points to where to start.

Feature IO YFT Your model What the converter does / where to look
SS3 version 3.24AB Tested on 3.24 only. ss3_read_model() reads the par file with SS_readpar_3.24(), and ss3_lencomp_n_mult() and the catch row of ss3_reconcile() expect 3.24 layouts. For 3.30, check every reader in ss3-convert.R, and ss3_recdevs().
Model period (SS3 years) 1-256 cfg$time; the opal step is the SS3 year.
Seasons per year 1 The converter assumes nseas = 1: opal gets n_season = 1, and ss3_catch_to_opal() keeps one catch value per year and fleet.
Months per season 3 Sets the M and K divisor (ss3_m_rate_divisor()).
Sexes 1 Single-sex only. ss3_endgrowth_table() keeps the first sex; two-sex compositions and spawning output need new code.
Areas 1 Single area only.
Ages (max) 28 cfg$age.
Fishing fleets 16 One opal fishery per SS3 fleet, in SS3 order.
Survey / index fleets 1 cfg$index (keep_ss3_fleets, split); opal adds one fishery per index series.
Catch units (1 biomass, 2 numbers) 2 Passed through (opal uses the same codes).
Index observations 176 ss3_index_to_opal(); negative fleet codes are dropped; scaled to mean 1.
Length composition rows 1114 ss3_lencomp_to_opal(); one sex, no partitions. mult_by_lencomp_N becomes lf_var_adjust.
Age composition rows 0 Not converted. Conditional age-at-length or age data need new code.
Generalised size comp methods 1 Not converted (IO YFT’s survey size data are dropped).
Tag release groups 0 Not converted.
Growth model (1 vB, 2 Richards, 3 age-K) 3 3: growth$model = "ss3_age_k" (exact). 1: "schnute", which matches von Bertalanffy. 2: Schnute approximation only; check the length-at-age row of ss3_reconcile().
Growth patterns 1 One expected.
Platoons per growth pattern 1 One expected. With platoons, ss3_endgrowth_table() averages rows without abundance weights and warns.
Length selectivity patterns 0 Any pattern works for the bridging test (selectivity is read from ageselex). For the final model, choose opal_type_f to suit SS3’s shapes and check the seeding RMSE.
Age selectivity patterns 12, 15, 20 As above.
Time-block designs 0 Only one year of selectivity is used (selectivity$reference_year). Time-varying selectivity is not represented.
F method 3 opal removes catch at the start of each step; the bridging test measures the effect.
Stock-recruit function 3 opal is Beverton–Holt; steepness and σR are read from the par file.
Report.sso available yes Required for the endgrowth route, selectivity, B0 and the bridging test.

The converter also assumes the following, which are not in the table:

  • Initial conditions. The converter starts the population unfished: initial F is effectively zero and there are no initial age deviations. If your model starts from a fished equilibrium (initial equilibrium catch or initial F), ss3_pars_to_opal() has to set log_init_F_f and the map has to estimate it.
  • Recruitment deviations. Early and main deviations are read from the par file (ss3_recdevs()), and SS3’s bias-adjustment ramp from Report.sso. Forecast deviations are ignored.
  • Parameters with environmental links, time variation or deviations (other than recruitment) are not converted. Their effects on selectivity and biology are captured only through the single reference year read from Report.sso.

A suggested order for a new model:

  1. Run ss3_model_features() and fill in the “Your model” column.
  2. Set up cfg and get ss3_to_opal() to run, extending the converter where the table says it needs to.
  3. Make tests 1 and 2 pass exactly before anything else.
  4. Run the bridging test and make the replay with SS3 timing match SS3.
  5. Only then set up the opal selectivity and fit.
